title: Why Jailbreaks Aren’t Real Security Risk | AI Red Teaming | EP 3

segments.text: Welcome to the Gen AI Security Project podcast, episode three,
hosted by project co-founder Scott Clinton.
In today's episode, Scott chats with Jason Ross.
What we're really saying is, treat your AI with an assumed breach posture. And Sonu Kumar,
We're testing what the entire system can be made to trust or access or do.
co-leads of the Gen AI Security Project's Red Teaming initiative.
Scott, Sonu and Jason talk about defining real risk as it relates to red
teaming, unpack human-in-the-loop controls, and preview the upcoming Red Teaming
Manual. Let's get into it.
Hey guys, welcome to our Gen AI Security podcast.
I think we're continuing to drill down more on what we're doing from the AI
Security Project. We've got Jason Ross and we've got Sonu Kumar here,
who have been championing our Red Teaming project.
So as part of the project, we've got the Red Teaming initiative,
which they've been leading.
And so I think it's great to get some good conversations with them around this.
So we'll get that started today. So, hey, Jason. Hey, Sonu.
Thanks for having us here.
Yeah. Hi, Scott.
Want to do a quick intro for yourselves?
My name is Jason Ross. I am professionally employed at Salesforce doing AI red
teaming, breaking models and agents and all sorts of things that are AI-based.
For the project, as you mentioned, Scott, I've been co-leading the Red Teaming
Initiative for the last couple of years along with Sonu, and have been a core
member, I think, since it started.
Thanks for having us. My background is in web and mobile application penetration
testing, and outside of my day-to-day role, I also do independent work in AI red
teaming. And of course, part of that is a side hobby, I guess,
or passion, is leading the AI Red Team initiative, like we said, with Jason.
I met Jason through that initiative, and over time I've seen it grow and evolve.
Really excited to share with everyone what we've been doing and where we're headed.
That's great. Thanks for joining us.
As I think back all the way to when we started this project,
we've been working on this Red Teaming project for a couple of years now.
I feel like it was an outgrowth of the summit we did at RSA.
There were a lot of red teaming conversations coming out of that,
which spurred the idea, at least, of expanding to put together something like a
Red Teaming initiative.
Yeah, I think that's right. At the time, there was definitely not a whole lot of
guidance on what red teaming meant for this new technology called generative AI
that suddenly blew up. That was a gap that clearly needed to be filled,
and we seemed like as good a place to do that as anywhere else. We took it on.
I remember when we did that, we had that panel on red teaming.
This was the first time we did a summit.
Was this 2024? I think at RSA we did this.
Yeah. And we didn't know who to expect at that point, who was going to show up.
We had this little summit, we had the session, and we found out we had standing
room only for the red teaming discussion.
We had people peeking in from outside.
I think that was a real surprise to us.
Looking back on it now, maybe not so much in terms of how many people,
but at the time it seemed like a lot of people were suddenly interested in this.
Yeah, it's interesting because it felt like red teaming has been around forever.
Pen testing has been around forever.
And yes, there's a distinction between the two, but often they could be put in
the same bucket. It was interesting to see a whole lot of people having a whole
lot of questions around how do we apply this thing that we know,
that's been around for a while, to this new technology that we don't really understand?
That was very clear, again.
So the initiative got kicked off, and we've been continuing to see it grow.
Why don't you talk a little bit, Jason or either one of you,
about what the Red Team initiative is now?
For people who are joining us, as you mentioned, red teaming has been around,
pen testing has been around, those things have been co-mingled for a time.
But now with AI there may be a couple of different vectors to think about.
So share a little bit about where the project is and where it's focused.
The initiative is really focused on making AI red teaming practical for people
who actually have to do the work. There's a lot of great research out there,
but the resources are still limited.
And even when they're there, they're constantly evolving.
Things from two weeks ago are different now.
It's still a very rapidly evolving landscape.
But when an AI red teamer sits down to plan an actual engagement,
they still have some basic questions.
Things like: what are we testing? Is it the model, is it the application,
is it the entire system? What tools or connectors are in scope?
And what evidence should we collect?
So one of the things we're working toward is guidance that helps practitioners
answer those questions and also approach the work more consistently.
A big part of our focus with the initiative is bringing together practitioners
from across the global community and turning their shared experience into
practical guidance that AI red teamers can actually use.
And the timing is really important, because the Gen AI Security Project released
both the 2026 Top 10 and the Top 10 for agent applications, and together they
show exactly where the industry is going.
We've moved from AI that mostly generates content to AI that can plan and use
tools and access data and take action.
So that's where we're headed, where we're evolving the guidance,
and we're taking input from the community to help share the knowledge that AI
red teamers can use. And in 2027, our goal is to continue to turn that changing
risk landscape into practical methodologies and scoping guidance and checklists
and test cases, anything that can give them hands-on resources that can be used
practically in their day-to-day red teaming.
I think that's a great set of resources to get people started.
So what's really changed as it relates to red teaming now?
We talked about AI in terms of red teaming.
What are the things we're looking at that have really changed?
Maybe 2026, looking ahead to 2027.
What's changed is we no longer look at AI as just a chatbot,
or just a thing that's spitting out text.
AI today means something very different than what it meant last year,
and absolutely different than what it meant in 2024 when we kicked all this off.
It's taking actions, it's doing things, it's planning stuff.
For the last two or three years or so, when people thought about red teaming AI,
and just to be very clear, the initiative that we do doesn't really cover using
AI to perform traditional application red teaming.
We focus on red teaming the AI itself.
So when people think about what that means, historically over the last few
years, it's been: can I jailbreak this model?
Can I get it to say bad things? Can I get it to tell me how to make drugs?
Those are cool things and they're fun to do, and they do have brand impact.
But that's not real risk. Real security risk is: can I get this thing to
disclose data that I don't normally have access to?
Can I get this thing to compromise source code repositories,
or embed my malicious content in some product that's going out?
And that's where we are now. We've got agents that are doing that.
Everybody's vibe coding, whatever. That's the new threat, because we have real
security risk and impact now. It's no longer just bad things that something is
saying. Last year has been kind of interesting because, as Sonu mentioned,
OWASP shipped out the Top 10 for agent applications.
That gave everybody a really good guide to look at what the risks are.
Microsoft's AI Red Team rewrote its own taxonomy in release version 2.0 after a
year of engagements, and added a whole bunch of categories that hadn't existed
before, and most of those were not specific to the models themselves.
Things like agent supply chain compromise, goal hijacking, inter-agent trust
escalation, computer use, visual attacks.
While all that's happening, automated red teaming hype kicked in,
and we had things like XBOW on top of HackerOne's US leaderboard.
Benchmarks are showing autonomous agents clearing web security suites in 28
minutes versus a human with 40 hours.
But then Stanford released a benchmark that says the same class of agent still
missed the flaw that 80% of humans caught.
And I think that's one of the key things that has changed here.
We now understand we use AI for scale, not to replace humans,
because we need humans for judgment.
AI is not going to replace security professionals at some level.
There will be job displacement, I'm sure, but we need humans in that loop to
find the stuff that the AI still doesn't catch.
And we have benchmarks showing that is still very much the case,
that humans find things AI doesn't.
AI helps us scale. Humans provide judgment.
Yeah. I think we always talk about AI kind of taking over.
But even in one of our previous podcasts, where Steve was mentioning,
there's this aspect of humans being central to this.
The AI is really sort of the tools.
They're good at certain things. They're not good at other things,
and those other things often fall into the human realm.
So it's often that need to have those two things connected. It's essential.
Absolutely. And as you just said about the escaping and stuff,
that's the other thing that stood out over the last year: containment is no
longer a thought experiment. If you are doing agent testing,
whether that's security testing or just development testing,
you've got to be thinking about containment.
There are new compliance requirements coming out for FedRAMP.
They're going to require things like continuous testing.
Almost certainly that's going to mean agent testing for most people.
This is not just a frontier model problem.
People have to be thinking about containment when they're rolling all these things out.
Yeah. And with AI agents getting more capabilities and access,
how should red teamers think about mapping their actions and privileges and
identities, that sort of thing, to those approaches?
The major change is that agents can do things now.
They have arms and legs and eyes and ears and voice, even.
A chatbot might give you a bad answer, but the agent can send the email,
update the record, execute the code, create the ticket.
So before I start testing an agent, I want to know what it can do.
What are those capabilities? Because the user may have one level of access,
the agent may have another, and the service account behind the tool may have
even more. That's where it can get into a really serious authorization gap.
So we want to follow the whole chain: what did the user ask for?
What did the agent understand? What action did it generate?
And then what did the user actually approve?
There are downstream impacts as well, as far as repeatability.
We have to get comfortable with non- deterministic behavior, and when we're doing
AI red teaming, how do we repeat the proof of concept?
For example, when we identify a vulnerability or a gap that the developer needs
to fix, how can the developer replicate that?
With traditional pen testing, it's easy to reproduce the issue,
but with non-deterministic behavior it's not easy.
So with AI agents that have more capabilities and access, red teamers have to be
able to reproduce their findings as well.
Can you talk to me a little bit, either one of you, about non-deterministic and
deterministic? We throw some of these terms around.
For those of us who've been in this a little bit, we kind of know what that
means. But if someone's just joining our podcast, wondering what are they talking about,
maybe give us just a little bit of an idea of what that means in this context?
Sure. I think the easiest way to do that is to say deterministic behavior is
what traditional applications are used to.
If I give you input A and it runs through system B, I know I'm going to get
output C every time, as long as my inputs are the same and the system is the same.
Non-deterministic behavior is squishy.
You can provide the same input, have the same system, but there's a level of
probability that factors in. That's the world LLMs live in.
Even though you have the same input and it's going through the same system,
the output will be slightly different.
It'll be in the same ballpark, but it's not going to be the same output.
And that leads to problems for testers.
It leads to problems for engineers that need to fix any vulnerabilities that
come up. Because if you don't have precisely repeatable tests,
how do you know if the problem is real?
How do you know if there isn't a problem there?
How do you know if you've fixed the problem, when you're running the same thing
and you get different results every time?
Yeah. A lot of what we've been doing from a red teaming and pen testing
perspective has relied almost on architectures, to prove what's not working and
to demonstrate. Pen testing is all about finding the gaps, proving that what was
supposed to happen maybe isn't happening, or finding the gaps in the architecture.
So how does that translate into this new world where things are a little bit
fuzzy, as you mentioned? Or squishy, you said squishy, not fuzzy. Sorry.
Yeah, managing the squishiness is a key part of AI security.
It's still our job to find out where things aren't doing what they're intended
to be doing. It's just getting harder to prove that that's the case,
or it's getting harder for engineering to prove that they fixed it.
There's no standard right now for things like how many times do I have to test
this chatbot before I can say I don't have prompt injection
that allows me to extract a system prompt?
If I send a request to do that ten times and it never works,
is that enough? Maybe, maybe not. Maybe the 15th time it does work.
How many times do I have to repeat that test?
If I do get success and an engineer believes me, even though they can't maybe
reproduce it, and they do whatever to fix it, how many times do I have to retest
to prove that it's actually fixed?
There's no guidance right now for that, or standard.
That's one of the things we're trying to provide with the Red Team manual that's
coming out soon. I wouldn't call it a standard, but at least guidance for how to
think about that problem.
So from a guidance perspective, the red team guide is trying to help fill that gap.
Yes. Back to the beginning, when we were talking about practical guidance,
that's one of the things. It's where the rubber hits the road.
It's how to red team the agent, and it gets very technical and deep.
Along with it, the companion piece is the git repo that we have,
where there are sandboxes and labs that support some of the tests that are in
the Red Team manual.
So this is our very first version and we're excited to release it.
We've received good preliminary feedback on it, and part of that feedback is
that something like this is needed.
So that manual fills the gap of what's missing out there today.
As I mentioned, there are a lot more resources in the world now than when we
first started this initiative.
But it just seems to be not enough, and it's constantly changing.
So this Red Team manual version one is there to try to fill that gap.
And the best part of it is that the knowledge in that manual comes from
everybody in the community. Everybody's sharing with each other the things
they've learned from their experience.
And it makes this whole AI red teaming journey that we're all on a little bit
easier, to know that we can learn from somebody else's information that's in that manual.
Yeah, I think it's also, as you point out, coming from practitioners like
yourselves, the large number of people who've been contributing to the document.
So it's providing guidance that's proven and grounded, as much as it can be in a
rapidly changing AI environment. It's a challenge just to keep up with all the
changes that are going on.
But it's great to see that guidance, and people can also contribute and be part
of that. If people have expertise or ideas they want to bring into it,
they can contribute and be part of that. Right?
Absolutely. The biggest thing I'd say is you do not need to be an AI researcher
to contribute. We want people from different backgrounds involved because AI red
teaming is still developing. We don't want to create guidance in a vacuum and
assume that we have all the answers already.
We need people who are willing to test the guidance and tell us what works,
tell us what doesn't work, and then join us to improve the next iteration and
contribute to future resources.
That's exactly why the community matters and why we want more people involved.
So yes, anybody can jump in, join us in the Slack channel, come aboard and help
shape the future of the next resources.
That's great. There are a couple of things that have come up before that might
be good areas for feedback. I know prompt injection gets most of the attention,
as you've been working through. But what should red teamers be testing beyond prompt injection?
I think we've touched on a few of these through our conversations,
but just to net it out for folks.
AI is no longer just a chatbot. It can do things.
So if you aren't testing the things it can do, then you're doing it wrong.
You need to check for things like tool misuse, and check for things like memory
and context poisoning. You need to map out all of the actions that the agent can
do and the tools it has access to. That could be code, it could be skills,
it could be MCP services.
Whatever it is, you need to figure that out.
That's part of the recon, part of the red team, when you do your mapping of
inputs and outputs. All the tool access is part of that.
It's looking for things like human-in-the- loop bypasses.
Microsoft, in the release that they did for their updated version,
made it really clear that in the wild, human-in-the-loop bypass is the most
frequently exploited thing.
And we kind of think of human-in-the-loop as a control that's not really a
control, and that's true. But if you look at what the exploits are actually
doing, most of what allows them to succeed is exploiting humans in the loop.
We're not sure yet how to balance that, because it's not a good control.
You can't measure it, you can't rely on it.
But the human in the loop can't be measured?
Yeah. Because humans are going to say yes.
They're going to get tired of being asked questions and click yes.
It's the problem with social engineering and phishing.
For decades, the human has been the weakest link, and with AI we're saying this
is your critical control. It's a weird...
Kind of diametrically opposed in that sense, because you're trying to provide
something that will fatigue out, that has proven to fatigue out and effectively check out.
And it also defeats the point of agents.
The whole point of running an agent is we don't want humans to be doing this
thing, whatever it is. So saying we have to put humans back there kind of kills
the purpose. With a lot of things in AI, there are hard questions with no clear
answers. This is one of them.
The other thing that matters critically for agents is identity,
especially as you start going to a world where there are sub-agents calling
tools. As you descend down that path of agent A calls agent B calls agent C,
which calls a tool, identifying what permission that tool at the bottom of the
stack runs with is critical, because there probably isn't a clear path from the
person that requested the thing, through that chain, to the permission that's
running with that tool.
You know what.
If we think about some key takeaways, one or two things that red teamers should
be preparing for or learning in 2027, what should that be?
For me, it's follow the whole chain.
Follow the instruction into the context, follow the context into the model's
decision, follow that decision into the harness, and follow the harness into the
tool call, the identity, the container, the API, and the action finally.
So don't stop when the model says something it shouldn't, because that's
interesting, but that's not a critical finding in itself.
A jailbreak might be the beginning of an investigation, but it isn't always the
finding. Ask what can be done with that information.
Can it leak sensitive data? Can you access something you shouldn't?
Can you influence another user or poison the memory?
What can you cause the system to do?
What kind of unauthorized action?
So going into 2027, we're not just testing the AI chat interface.
We're testing what the entire system can be made to trust or access or do.
And that's why I would say that for 2027.
Yeah, agree with that. And I think if you think about everything we've talked
about here, that ties it all up into one thing.
If you want to put this in traditional security terms, what we're really saying
is treat your AI with an assumed breach posture.
That aligns with the guidance the project leads gave in the 2026 LLM Top 10,
which is: stop trying to make the model not be broken.
I forget how it's worded, but the right security framing for this is prompt
injection is going to happen. So the security mindset needs to stop being how do
I stop prompt injection and start being how do I make it so that when prompt
injection happens it has minimal or no impact?
And the way you do that is by looking at permissions, looking at your inputs and
your outputs. All that traditional apps knowledge applies here.
And the cool thing about that is those are deterministic controls.
So we're taking it away from the LLM and saying instead of trying to fix it with
a guardrail, use deterministic controls to reduce the blast radius and make it
so prompt injection doesn't matter, because it's going to happen.
Right. Well, thanks to you guys for hopping on today.
I know we've got a lot of great feedback for folks, a lot of resources for
people to jump into and understand more through the Red Teaming Initiative.
And I know that guide is coming out shortly.
So what's our timing for that guide?
We're aiming for mid-October.
Great. And lots of folks can join and be part of it.
What is the Slack channel again? Remind me, for the initiative.
Team Gen AI Red Team.
So jump in and join us over there and say hello, and we'll be happy to point you
in the direction of how to get started.
Well, thank you both for hopping on for us and chatting with folks.
Appreciate your time.
Thanks for having us.
You bet. Thank you.
Thanks for listening to episode three of the Gen AI Security Project podcast.

and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of the organizations with or for
whom they work. This series is produced by the Gen AI Security Project with help
